definition: In statistics and machine learning, leakage (also known as data leakage or target leakage) refers to the use of information during model training that would not be available at prediction time.
details: This results in overly optimistic performance estimates, as the model appears to perform better during evaluation than it actually would in a production environment. Leakage is often subtle and indirect, making it difficult to detect and eliminate. It can lead a statistician or modeler to select a suboptimal model, which may be outperformed by a leakage-free alternative.

explainer.lead: Leakage is the use of information during training that would not be available at prediction time. It produces overly optimistic performance estimates that do not hold in production.

tiers.eli5: Like studying for a test with the answer key in hand, then being surprised when the real exam is harder.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers guard against it by splitting data before any preprocessing and by auditing features for future information; the pitfall is that leakage is often subtle and indirect, so it is hard to detect.
tiers.paperLevel: Leakage means training uses information unavailable at prediction time; it inflates evaluation results and can lead to selecting a suboptimal model that a leakage-free alternative would outperform.

explainer.example: Computing normalization statistics over the full dataset, including the test set, before splitting makes the model look better in evaluation than in production.
